deep.reconstruction:
The page is a printed German algebra textbook in Fraktur type, not Gauss's handwriting. It was presumably bound or interleaved into the Gauss bundle. On the facing pages Gauss's own notes are the beta-integral substitution (previous page) and faint pencil marginalia (next page). This page holds only textbook worked examples of linear equations ax=b (the next page refers to §176 'ax-b=0').

(3, continued) Ox-fodder problem. Fodder suffices for 20 oxen for 12 months, i.e. 240 ox-months. More oxen arrive later: 5 more after 2 months and 10 more after a further 6.6 months, so 8.6 months after the start (inferred from the offsets). Let x be the duration for the first 20 oxen. Then the 5 feed x-2 months and the 10 feed x-8.6 months.
- Fundamental equation: 20x + 5(x-2) + 10(x-8.6) = 20*12.
- So 35x - 96 = 240 and x = 336/35 = 9 3/5 months.
- The last 10 oxen stay x - 8.6 = 1 month.

(4) Two brothers divide 4800 rthl. Each time the first takes 5, the second takes 4, and the second also gets 300 extra. Let x be the number of takings.
- 5x + 4x + 300 = 4800, so 9x = 4500 and x = 500.
- First brother: 5*500 = 2500. Second: 4*500 + 300 = 2300.

(Remark) Fox and hound with equal leap length. The fox has 60 leaps head start and makes 4 leaps while the hound makes 6. Let x be the number of such time units.
- Equation (implicit, mine): 6x = 60 + 4x, so x = 30.
- The hound catches the fox after 6*30 = 180 leaps.

(5) Pythagoras' pupils: (1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4)x = (13/12)x = x + 3.
- So 13x = 12x + 36 and x = 36.
- The book offers an alternative setup, '(13/12)(x-3) = x', to show the equation can be set up in different ways.

(6) Inheritance problem (stated here, solved on the next page). With estate x, the sons receive x/2 - 1000, x/3 - 800 and x/4 - 600, whose sum is x.
- So (13/12)x - 2400 = x and x = 28800.
- Shares: 13400, 8800, 6600.
errors: Problem 5: the alternative setup '(13/12)(x-3) = x' as printed gives 13x - 39 = 12x, i.e. x = 39, not 36. A consistent alternative is (12/13)(x+3) = x or (13/12)x - 3 = x. This is a slip or misprint in the textbook (the image shows odd brackets around x-3).
All other computations on the page (x = 9 3/5, x = 500 with 2500/2300, x = 30 with 180 leaps, x = 36) are correct.
Not on this page, but noted for context: the next page misprints the second son's share as '1/3x - 300' instead of 1/3x - 800. The following sum correctly uses 800.

results.what: Elementary word problems (fodder/ox-months, division of money, fox and hound pursuit, Pythagoras' pupils, inheritance) reduced to a linear equation ax = b
results.modern_name: Solving linear equations in one unknown; classical recreational and commercial arithmetic problems
results.usually_credited_to: Traditional (medieval and Renaissance Rechenbücher; e.g. pursuit problems go back to Fibonacci's Liber Abaci, and Pythagoras-pupil epigrams to the Greek Anthology)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a printed page of a standard 18th/19th-century German elementary algebra textbook with routine linear-equation exercises. Nothing on it is by Gauss or mathematically non-trivial.

checkable.asserts: The last 10 oxen are fed for 1 month
Brothers problem: x = 500, so shares 2500 and 2300
Fox and hound: x = 30, hound needs 180 leaps
The printed alternative setup gives 39, not 36, so it is a slip

transcription_corrections: The page is printed (Fraktur typeset), not a Gauss manuscript; the transcription of the text is otherwise essentially accurate.
In problem 5 the alternative equation is printed with irregular brackets around (x - 3); the content '13/12 (x-3) = x' is as printed, though mathematically inconsistent.
The footer 'F 3' is the printer's signature mark, and 'Die' is the catchword for the next page.
